raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, chills and one episode of vomiting. On admission, he had a single seizure episode, followed by an altered sensorium and deteriorating neurological status. He also had an erythematous macular rash over his body. The patient tested positive for dengue non-structural (NS1) antigen and immunoglobulin M (IgM) dengue antibody, while the test for dengue immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody was negative. The haematological investigations at the time of presentation revealed a reduced haemoglobin (7 gm/dL) and thrombocytopaenia with a platelet count of 60 000/microl, which reduced to 40 000/microl over the subsequent two days. The platelet count steadily improved thereafter and was 80 000/microl on the sixth day.
CT imaging of the brain (Figures 1a-c) revealed ill-defined symmetrical bilateral hypodensities in the thalami, cerebellar white matter and bilateral frontal subcortical and deep white matter. Tiny hyperdense haemorrhagic foci were observed within some of these hypodense areas (Figure 1c). Repeat CT Brain imaging (Figures 1d-f), performed a day later due to the patient's clinical deterioration, revealed an increase in the haemorrhagic foci with intraventricular extension, obstructive hydrocephalus and generalized cerebral oedema.
MRI of the brain (Figures 2a-i) performed on the second day of admission revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, hyperintense areas on fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T2-weighted images involving the thalami, cerebellum, bilateral frontal and parietal subcortical and deep white matter, with patchy restricted diffusion at diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) (Figure 2g). Multiple internal foci of blooming were seen on gradient recalled echoplanar (GRE) images, representing haemorrhages (Figures 2h and 2i).
A diagnosis of dengue-associated haemorrhagic encephalitis was made based on the clinical presentation, imaging and laboratory findings.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever, chills, and vomiting for five days, complicated by an acute seizure and deteriorating sensorium.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 25-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, chills, and one episode of emesis. On admission, he experienced a single seizure followed by acute sensorium alteration and rapidly progressive neurological deterioration. He also displayed a generalized erythematous macular rash. Hematology revealed progressive thrombocytopenia followed by gradual recovery over six days.
subjective.review_of_systems: Emesis, chills; no focal motor symptoms preceding seizure.

objective.physical_examination: Altered sensorium with deteriorating neurological status; generalized erythematous macular skin rash.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 7 gm/dL, platelet count 60,000/microL on presentation, dropping to 40,000/microL over the subsequent 2 days, and improving to 80,000/microL on day 6.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT (admission): Ill-defined symmetrical bilateral hypodensities in the thalami, cerebellar white matter, and bilateral frontal subcortical and deep white matter, with tiny hyperdense hemorrhagic foci. Repeat Brain CT (day 2): Increase in hemorrhagic foci with intraventricular hemorrhage extension, obstructive hydrocephalus, and generalized cerebral edema. Brain MRI (day 2): Multiple bilaterally symmetrical hyperintense areas on T2/FLAIR involving the thalami, cerebellum, and bilateral frontal and parietal subcortical/deep white matter, patchy diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC, and multiple foci of blooming on GRE images confirming parenchymal hemorrhages.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus hemorrhagic encephalitis complicated by intraventricular hemorrhage, obstructive hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, severe thrombocytopenia, and anemia. Confirmed by positive Dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen and positive Dengue IgM antibody, with negative Dengue IgG antibody.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted for emergent neurocritical care and supportive management with intracranial pressure monitoring, anti-edema measures, blood component support, and neurological observation, achieving platelet stabilization and neurological monitoring.
